source_text: Παντὶ τοίνυν σθένει ὁ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος παιδαγωγός, ὁ θεῖος ἡμῶν λόγος, πάσῃ καταχρώμενος σοφίας μηχανῇ, σῴζειν ἐπιβέβληται τοὺς νηπίους, νουθετῶν, ἐπιτιμῶν, ἐπιπλήττων, ἐλέγχων, ἀπειλούμενος, ἰώμενος, ἐπαγγελλόμενος, χαριζόμενος, »πολλοῖς τισιν οἱονεὶ χαλινοῖς« τὰς ἀλόγους τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος »δεσμεύων« ὁρμάς. συνελόντι γοῦν εἰπεῖν, οὕτως ὁ κύριος πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸς τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν. »τέκνα σοί ἐστιν; παίδευσον αὐτά«, ἡ σοφία παραινεῖ, »καὶ κάμψον αὐτὰ ἐκ νεότητος αὐτῶν. θυγατέρες σοί εἰσι; πρόσεχε τῷ σώματι αὐτῶν, καὶ μὴ ἱλαρώσῃς πρὸς αὐτὰς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου.« καίτοι τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν, υἱούς τε καὶ θυγατέρας, σφόδρα καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὁτιοῦν ἀγαπῶμεν. ἐπεὶ δ᾿ οἱ μὲν πρὸς χάριν ὁμιλοῦντες ὀλίγον ἀγαπῶσιν ὃ μὴ λυποῦσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς ὠφέλειαν ἐπιστύφοντες, εἰ καὶ παραυτίκα λυπηροί, ἀλλὰ εἰς τὸν ἔπειτα εὐεργετοῦσιν αἰῶνα, οὐ τὴν παραυτίκα ἡδονὴν ὁ κύριος, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέλλουσαν ἐσκόπησε τρυφήν. ἐπίωμεν δὲ ἤδη καὶ τὸν τρόπον αὐτοῦ τῆς φιλανθρώπου παιδαγωγίας μετὰ μαρτυρίας προφητικῆς. Νουθέτησις μὲν οὖν ἐστιν ψόγος κηδεμονικός, νοῦ ἐμποιητικός. τοιοῦτος ὁ παιδαγωγὸς νουθετῶν, ὡς κἀν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ λέγων »ποσάκις ἠθέλησα συναγαγεῖν τὰ τέκνα σου, ὃν τρόπον ὄρνις συνάγει τὰ νοσσία αὐτῆς ὑπὸ τὰς πτέρυγας αὐτῆς, καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε«. αὖθίς τε ἡ γραφὴ νουθετεῖ, »καὶ ἐμοίχευον« λέγουσα »τὸ ξύλον καὶ τὸν λίθον, καὶ ἐθυμίασαν τῇ Βάαλ«. μέγιστον γὰρ τεκμήριον τῆς φιλανθρωπίας αὐτοῦ, ὅτι καίτοι σαφῶς εἰδὼς τὴν ἀναισχυντίαν τοῦ ἐκλακτίσαντος λαοῦ καὶ ἀποσκιρτήσαντος, ὅμως ἐπὶ τὴν μετάνοιαν παρακαλεῖ καί φησιν διὰ τοῦ Ἰεζεκιήλ· »υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου, ἐν μέσῳ σκορπίων σὺ κατοικεῖς, πλὴν λάλησον αὐτοῖς, ἐὰν ἄρα ἀκούσωσιν.« ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ Μωυσεῖ »πορεύου« φησὶν »καὶ εἰπὲ τῷ Φαραώ, ἵνα ἐξαποστείλῃ τὸν λαόν, ἐγὼ δὲ οἶδα ὅτι οὐ μὴ ἐξαποστείλῃ αὐτούς«. ἐμφαίνει γὰρ ἄμφω, καὶ τὸ θεῖον προειδὼς τὸ ἐσόμενον, καὶ τὸ φιλάνθρωπον τὸ αὑτοῦ τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀφορμὰς μετανοίας χαριζόμενος. νουθετεῖ δὲ καὶ διὰ Ἡσαΐου κηδόμενος τοῦ λαοῦ, ὁπηνίκα λέγει· »ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τοῖς χείλεσιν αὐτῶν τιμῶσί με, ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἐστὶν ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ« (τοῦτό ἐστι ψόγος ἐλεγκτικός)· »μάτην δὲ σέβονταί με διδάσκοντες διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων.« ἐνταῦθα ἡ κηδεμονία φανερώσασα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ παραλλήλου δείκνυσι τὴν σωτηρίαν. Ἐπιτίμησις δέ ἐστι ψόγος ἐπ᾿ αἰσχροῖς οἰκειῶν πρὸς τὰ καλά. τοῦτο ἐνδείκνυται διὰ Ἱερεμίου· »ἵπποι θηλυμανεῖς ἐγενήθησαν, ἕκαστος ἐπὶ τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ ἐχρεμέτιζεν. μὴ ἐπὶ τούτοις οὐκ ἐπισκέψομαι; λέγει κύριος· ἢ ἐν λαῷ τῷ τοιούτῳ οὐκ ἐκδικήσει ἡ ψυχή μου;« παραπλέκει δὲ πανταχοῦ τὸν φόβον, ὅτι »φόβος κυρίου ἀρχὴ αἰσθήσεως«. καὶ πάλιν διὰ Ὠσηὲ »οὐκ ἐπισκέψομαι« φησίν »αὐτούς· ὅτι αὐτοὶ μετὰ τῶν πορνῶν συνεφύροντο καὶ μετὰ τῶν τετελεσμένων ἔθυον, καὶ ὁ λαὸς ὁ συνίων συνεπλέκετο πόρνῃ«. δείκνυσιν αὐτῶν φανερώτερον τὸ ἁμάρτημα, συνιέναι αὐτοὺς ὁμολογῶν, ὡς ἑκόντας ἁμαρτάνοντας. καὶ ἡ σύνεσις ὄψις ἐστὶ ψυχῆς. διὸ καὶ ὁ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ ὁρῶν τὸν θεόν, τουτέστιν ὁ συνίων τὸν θεόν. Μέμψις δέ ἐστι ψόγος ὡς ὀλιγωρούντων ἢ ἀμελούντων. κέχρηται τῷ τρόπῳ τούτῳ τῆς παιδαγωγίας διὰ Ἡσαΐου λέγων· »ἄκουε, οὐρανέ, καὶ ἐνωτίζου, γῆ, ὅτι κύριος ἐλάλησεν· υἱοὺς ἐγέννησα καὶ ὕψωσα, αὐτοὶ δέ με ἠθέτησαν. ἔγνω βοῦς τὸν κτησάμενον καὶ ὄνος τὴν φάτνην τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ, Ἰσραὴλ δέ με οὐκ ἔγνω.« πῶς γὰρ οὐ δεινόν, εἰ ὁ εἰδὼς τὸν θεὸν οὐ γνώσεται τὸν κύριον, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν βοῦς καὶ ὁ ὄνος, τὰ νωθῆ ζῷα καὶ τὰ μωρά, εἴσεται τὸν τρέφοντα, ὁ δὲ Ἰσραὴλ ἀλογώτερος καὶ τούτων εὑρεθήσεται; καὶ διὰ Ἱερεμίου πολλὰ καταμεμψάμενος τὸν λαὸν ἐπιφέρει· »καὶ ἐμὲ ἐγκατέλιπον, λέγει κύριος.« Ἐπίπληξις δέ ἐστιν ἐπιτίμησις ἐπιπληκτικὴ ἢ ψόγος πληκτικός, κέχρηται δὲ καὶ ταύτῃ τῇ θεραπείᾳ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς διὰ Ἡσαΐου λέγων· »οὐαὶ τέκνα ἀποστάται, τάδε λέγει κύριος· ἐποιήσατε βουλὴν οὐ δι᾿ ἐμοῦ, καὶ συνθήκας οὐ διὰ τοῦ πνεύματός μου.« στύμματι δὲ αὐστηροτάτῳ παρ᾿ ἕκαστα προσχρῆται τῷ φόβῳ, ἀναστομῶν ἅμα καὶ ἐπιστρέφων δι᾿ αὐτοῦ πρὸς σωτηρίαν τὸν λαόν, καθάπερ καὶ τὰ βαπτόμενα τῶν ἐρίων προστύφεσθαι φιλεῖ εἰς βεβαίαν εὐτρεπιζόμενα τῆς βαφῆς παραδοχήν. Ἔλεγχος δέ ἐστιν προφορὰ ἁμαρτίας εἰς τὸ μέσον φέρουσα.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the divine Logos, our Pedagogue, using every device of wisdom, has been entrusted to save the infants, by admonishing, rebuking, striking, convicting, threatening, healing, promising, and granting favors, as it were, with many reins, binding the irrational impulses of humanity. To put it briefly, the Lord is to us as we are to our children. Wisdom advises, 'If you have children, discipline them, and bend them from their youth. If you have daughters, pay attention to their bodies, and do not smile at them.' Although we love our children, both sons and daughters, extremely and more than anything, those who associate with them for pleasure love them little, because they do not grieve them, whereas those who are concerned for their benefit, even if they cause them grief for the moment, nevertheless benefit them for the future age. The Lord did not consider present pleasure, but future delight. Let us follow also the manner of His philanthropic pedagogy, with prophetic testimony. Admonition is a paternal rebuke, imparting mind. Such is the Pedagogue, admonishing, as also in the Gospel, saying, 'How often I wanted to gather your children, as a bird gathers its nestlings under its wings, and you were not willing.' Again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, 'They committed adultery with the tree and the stone, and they burned incense to Baal.' For the greatest proof of His philanthropy is that, although He clearly knew the shamelessness of the people who were erring and revolted, He nevertheless calls them to repentance and says through Ezekiel, 'Son of man, you dwell among scorpions; speak to them, if perhaps they will listen.' And to Moses, He says, 'Go and tell Pharaoh to let the people go, but I know he will not let them go.' For He shows both the divine foreknowledge of what is to come and the philanthropic intention of giving them opportunities for repentance. He also admonishes through Isaiah, caring for the people, when He says, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me' (this is a reproachful rebuke); 'but in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' Here, the pedagogy, having revealed the sin, shows the salvation by analogy. Rebuke is a rebuke on account of shameful things, belonging to the good. This is shown through Jeremiah: 'The horses have become lustful stallions, each one neighing after his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things?' says the Lord, 'or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?' He also brings fear everywhere, because 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of perception.' And again, through Hosea, He says, 'I will not punish them, for they have mixed with prostitutes and sacrificed with the initiated, and the people who understand have been entangled with a prostitute.' He shows their sin more clearly, confessing that they understand, as if they were sinning willingly. And understanding is the vision of the soul. Therefore, Israel, who sees God, that is, who understands God. Blame is a rebuke as if they were neglecting or being careless. The Pedagogue uses this method of pedagogy through Isaiah, saying, 'Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know me.' For how is it not terrible, if one who knows God does not recognize the Lord, but the ox and the donkey, dull and foolish animals, know their feeder, and Israel is found to be more irrational than these? And through Jeremiah, having blamed the people much, He brings, 'And they have forsaken me,' says the Lord. Conviction is a reproachful rebuke or a striking rebuke. The Pedagogue also uses this treatment through Isaiah, saying, 'Woe to the apostate children,' thus says the Lord, 'you have made a plan not through me, and a covenant not through my Spirit.' With the most severe threat, He uses fear for each thing, at the same time turning and converting the people to salvation through it, just as the wool that is being dyed is also roughened, so that it may be firmly fixed in the reception of the dye. Conviction is the bringing of sin into the open.

pass_b_english: Therefore the divine Logos, our Pedagogue, employing every device of wisdom, is charged with saving the infants. He admonishes, rebukes, strikes, convicts, threatens, heals, promises, and grants favors, and, as it were, with many reins he binds the irrational impulses of humanity. To put it briefly, the Lord relates to us exactly as we relate to our own children. Wisdom advises, 'If you have children, discipline them, and bend them from their youth. If you have daughters, pay attention to their bodies, and do not smile at them' (Sirach 7:23–26). Although we love our children, both sons and daughters, extremely and more than anything, those who associate with them for pleasure love them little, because they do not grieve them, whereas those who are concerned for their benefit, even if they cause them grief for the moment, nevertheless benefit them for the age to come. The Lord did not look to present pleasure, but to the future delight. Let us now follow the manner of His philanthropic pedagogy, with prophetic testimony. Admonition is a paternal rebuke that imparts understanding. Such is the Pedagogue when He admonishes, as also in the Gospel He says, 'How often I wanted to gather your children, as a bird gathers its nestlings under its wings, and you were not willing' (Matthew 23:37). Again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, 'They committed adultery with the tree and the stone, and they burned incense to Baal' (Hosea 11:1–2). For the greatest proof of His philanthropy is that, although He clearly knew the shamelessness of the people who were erring and revolting, He nevertheless calls them to repentance and says through Ezekiel, 'Son of man, you dwell among scorpions; speak to them, if perhaps they will listen' (Ezekiel 2:3–4). And to Moses He says, 'Go and tell Pharaoh to let the people go, but I know he will not let them go' (Exodus 3:19). For He shows both the divine foreknowledge of what is to come and the philanthropic intention of giving them opportunities for repentance. He also admonishes through Isaiah, caring for the people, when He says, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me' (this is a reproachful rebuke); 'but in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' (Isaiah 29:13). Here the pedagogy, having revealed the sin, shows the salvation by analogy. Rebuke is a rebuke on account of shameful things, belonging to the good. This is shown through Jeremiah: 'The horses have become lustful stallions, each one neighing after his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?' (Jeremiah 5:8–9). He also brings fear everywhere, because 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of perception' (Proverbs 1:7). And again, through Hosea, He says, 'I will not punish them, for they have mixed with prostitutes and sacrificed with the initiated, and the people who understand have been entangled with a prostitute' (Hosea 4:14). He shows their sin more clearly, confessing that they understand, as if they were sinning willingly. And understanding is the vision of the soul. Therefore, Israel who sees God, that is, who understands God. Blame is a rebuke as if they were neglecting or being careless. The Pedagogue uses this method of pedagogy through Isaiah, saying, 'Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know me' (Isaiah 1:2–3). For how is it not terrible, if one who knows God does not recognize the Lord, but the ox and the donkey, dull and foolish animals, know their feeder, and Israel is found to be more irrational than these? And through Jeremiah, having blamed the people much, He adds, 'And they have forsaken me,' says the Lord (Jeremiah 2:13). Conviction is a reproachful rebuke or a striking rebuke. The Pedagogue also uses this treatment through Isaiah, saying, 'Woe to the apostate children,' thus says the Lord, 'you have made a plan not through me, and a covenant not through my Spirit' (Isaiah 30:1). With the most severe threat He uses fear for each thing, at the same time turning and converting the people to salvation through it, just as the wool that is being dyed is also roughened, so that it may be firmly fixed in the reception of the dye. Conviction is the bringing of sin into the open.
